newsitem.title: BELGIUM: France finally hands Dassault documents to Belgium.
newsitem.headline: France finally hands Dassault documents to Belgium.

text.p: France on Friday finally handed Belgium a series of documents relating to an alleged bribery scandal involving French aviation firm Dassault and Belgian political parties.

The handover of the nine documents, promised on Wednesday by French President Jacques Chirac, brings to a close a long-running diplomatic dispute that has soured relations between the two countries for the past 18 months.

"The documents in the Dassault case were transferred today from the French Justice Ministry to the Cour de Cassation in Brussels which examined them and established that they were the papers that had been promised," a Belgian Justice Ministry spokesman said.

Two other documents that had been requested by Belgium were held back. The French Justice Ministry said the two could harm French national security -- an argument invoked by the former centre-right government for withholding all the documents.
Justice Minister Elisabeth Guigou, who came to office after a Socialist-led election win on June 1, called the handover an "important step" in bolstering judicial cooperation in the European Union.
Dassault is suspected of having paid a total of 600 million Belgian francs ($16 million) in bribes to Belgian political parties in the late 1980s in return for contracts to refit F16 jet fighters.
The firm has denied any wrongdoing.
The affair forced the resignation of three government ministers in 1993 and of NATO Secretary General Willy Claes in 1994.
Claes, who was economics minister in the late 1980s, and the others have consistently denied knowledge of the alleged bribes.
However, investigators have discovered several secret bank accounts in Luxembourg belonging to Belgian political parties, and traced quantities of money to the Dassault affair.
Last month Belgium withdrew an international arrest warrant for company chief Serge Dassault.
The warrant was issued in July last year after the influential and well-connected industrialist had refused to come to Belgium to be interviewed by the Liege magistrate investigating the affair.
Time has started running out for the Belgian investigators who, under the country's statute of limitations, have until the end of September 1998 to conclude the case.
